rows.12:c2f8:
Every day, he filmed the bullying with a hidden camera.
(This is awful...)
That's what he thought to himself.
But he never once stepped in to stop it.
I suppose he felt it would mean more to finish this footage and deal with the root of the problem than to fix just the tip of the iceberg.
He narrowed the documentary down to one particular bullied student.
From then on, he followed that student every single day.
But it's a strange thing. The bullying that had seemed so awful to him at first gradually became nothing more than a subject for his lens.{p}
rows.12:c508: Then one day, that student jumped off the roof and killed himself.
rows.12:c548:
Tokita was filming it, of course.
They say that as the student fell, he noticed Tokita and looked sadly into the camera.{p}
rows.12:c6b0:
How should he edit the footage he'd shot?
He thought it over.
Then he asked the members of the film society for help and decided to turn it into a comic film.
He would raise the problem through laughter. That was his idea.{p}
rows.12:c774:
He started editing.
Editing is a kind of sorcery, isn't it?
With cheerful music, sound effects and the way the film is spliced together, grim footage of bullying turns into a comedy.
Though it also helped that the society members really knew what they were doing.{p}
rows.12:c858:
The comedy was shown at the school festival.
The audience laughed a lot, you know.
Without knowing it was a tragedy that had really happened.
Maybe the truly frightening thing is the crowd, people like that.
As long as they think it's fiction, they can laugh at someone else's misery.
No, even if they knew it was true, they might still laugh.
I even started to feel that way.{p}
rows.12:c9a4:
After the film, the staff were introduced.
The audience applauded loudly.
"That was a wonderful comedy."
Tokita tried to say something to the emcee who'd said that.
This isn't just a comedy.
I suppose that's what he was feeling.
But his hesitant attempt was soon drowned out by the cheers of the audience.
I could read Tokita's feelings as clearly as if I held them in my hand.
If he told them the film's true meaning now, wouldn't it kill the mood?
Wouldn't the cheers turn into complaints...?
And so Tokita answered the audience's applause with a broad smile.
People's attitudes really do change in front of a crowd, don't they?{p}
rows.12:cbd4:
After that, Tokita ended up making a second installment of the comedy.
Apparently the school was paying for the production, so he was trying to gather good equipment.
He seemed to be having the time of his life.
His only goal became making films that would go over well. Nothing else.{p}
rows.12:ccd4:
Then one day, inexplicable accidents began to happen.
The friends who'd helped edit his film had accidents, one after another.
Besides them, plenty of other students had accidents too.
Traffic accidents, injuries in P.E. class... though none of them were life-threatening.
Tokita thought, could it be...?
He took out the staff notes from the school festival and the list of audience members, and checked the names.
"I knew it. The people whose names are written here are the ones having accidents."
At that point, it never even occurred to him that he himself was at the center of this film.{p}
rows.12:cec8:
Tokita picked up his video camera and set out to interview the victims.
Just then, he sensed something and turned around.{p}
rows.12:cf68:
"Y-you're..."
Standing there was the student who'd killed himself, the one he'd filmed for the first comedy.
Tokita sank to the floor in terror.
"What did you make that film for?"{p}
rows.12:d024:
So said the student's ghost.
"And what kind of film are you making now?"
The pale-faced ghost reached out toward Tokita.
Tokita couldn't say a thing.
The spot between his eyes burned with fear, and tears welled up.
The ghost touched the video camera in Tokita's hand.
And then..................{p}
rows.12:d154:
The next day, Tokita was found dead in the newspaper club's room.
This very club room, I mean.
It's better if I don't describe the body.
You might not be able to eat your dinner tonight.
I'll just say it was a pretty gruesome death.
Tokita's death must have been the grudge of the student who killed himself.
But why did he curse the people who showed the film and laughed at it, instead of the students who bullied him?
Grudges are strange things, aren't they?
Huh? How do I know this story, you ask?
After Tokita died, I found a videotape in this room, and on it, his interviews and his death were recorded with a comic touch.
There wasn't the slightest trace of sadness or fear in that footage.
{a}, you'd better not take your newspaper club work too far.
This seven wonders project of yours is material that won't stay just a joke, either.
That's the end of my story.
Next, please.{p}
rows.12:d48c:
...I see.
Once you get interested in the making side of films, you may not be able to simply enjoy watching them anymore.
That may differ from person to person, though...
So, let's say, hypothetically, you were going to work in film.
Well, it's only hypothetical, so just answer casually.
{a}, which one would you choose?{p}
rows.12:d5b0:
I thought so.
{a}, you like to be in the spotlight, don't you?
Actors stand out more than anyone, after all. It's flashy, glamorous work.
And the actors are the ones who get popular, too.{p}
rows.12:d658:
But it's hard work.
Because it's what people see, skill or the lack of it shows more than anywhere else.
The actors I think are amazing can handle any role flawlessly.
Well, that's how actors are supposed to be, of course.
...Tokita wanted to be the director.
Apparently that was settled without any fuss.{p}
rows.12:d774:
A cameraman?
How faithfully can you capture what the director asks for, following the storyboards?
With what sensibility do you express the work through the camera?
When the director or the producer says it's no good, you reshoot it again and again...
I'd think you have to push your own opinions with the staff, yet still stay obedient.
When you think about it like that, it seems pretty difficult.
After all, if all it took was pointing the camera, anyone could do it.
Most people choose a film by its actors or director.
I won't say nobody goes to see a film because of who the cameraman is, but there can't be many.
It's not that he wanted to stand out, but Tokita wanted to be the director.
He'd wanted to direct for a long time, after all.
Apparently no one objected.{p}
rows.12:da4c:
That's the person who oversees everything: the money, the overall schedule, the image of the work, their own vision.
Of all these jobs... well, it's questionable whether you can even call it a job, but it's the one with the most say, isn't it?
If it were just putting up the production money and leaving the rest to everyone else, it would be easy, but grasping the whole thing and overseeing it must be tough.
Every one of these jobs is tough, though.
It's a work you're producing with your own money, so you can't do it halfway.
If the production drags on, you might be so anxious and worried that you never get a moment's peace.
It seems like a job full of worries.
Tokita wanted to be the director.
Apparently no one objected.{p}
rows.12:dcc4:
A screenwriter?
That seems to call for writing skill.
On that point, {a}, as a reporter for the newspaper club, you seem used to writing.
Then there's the dialogue, building the story, meetings with the film's director, getting your ideas across...
But it sounds like hard work.
It seems you can't just write the script and say, 'There, the rest is up to you all...'
Well, that's obvious, of course.
Tokita wanted to be the director.
Apparently no one objected.{p}
rows.12:de70:
My, that's a rather understated choice.
When we say 'the crew behind the scenes,' that covers sets, props and so on.
There seem to be even finer divisions, but I'll skip those this time.
As the name says, I think it's plain, grueling work where you never step out front yourselves.
But when something turns out unexpectedly well, better than you'd hoped, it must make you really happy.
They say many people in those jobs are very particular.
Whatever they do, they never forget their own standards...
In a sense, they're artists, I suppose.
I think that devotion is what makes the things they create all the better.
In the society, there wasn't really a proper crew for sets and props.
The members took care of it themselves, making things or bringing them from home.{p}
rows.12:e158:
Tokita was the director.
It seems he'd wanted to direct for a long time.
He was also personally good at sculpting and modeling, so he seemed confident about props and makeup as well.
No one in particular objected to him directing.
And so the shooting of the society's memorable first production began.
I think it was right around this time last year.{p}
rows.12:e2c8:
The film he set out to make was a horror movie titled 'The Mummy Man and the Beauty.'
...Who's that laughing?
Admittedly, it's a cheesy-sounding title.
But it's a shame to laugh like that.
Tokita was truly giving it everything he had.
He studied hard how to create the most effective scenes on a limited budget.
The guys who'd seemed eager at first gradually got bored, as they do.
In the end, they only did what they wanted to and wouldn't touch anything that didn't interest them or was hard work.
Most of them had joined half for fun, after all.{p}
rows.12:e59c:
A mummy brought over from Egypt comes back to life and searches for the reincarnation of the princess he once served.
In the end, he turns her into a mummy too, puts her in his coffin with him, and the two of them return to Egypt...
Since they were all amateurs, the shoot seems to have been rough.
Eventually, one way or another, the shooting was finished.{p}
rows.12:e6ec:
But that's when the real trouble started.
You probably think a film is done once it's shot, but you'd be dead wrong.
Whether it turns out entertaining or not depends on the editing that comes next.
You take the scattered scenes on all the film you've shot and splice them together one by one.
And then a single film is complete.
Apparently it's work that takes a lot of patience.
Though for people who love it, I imagine it's irresistibly fun.
And Tokita was one of them, but...{p}
rows.12:e8bc:
Somehow, once he started editing, it was quite different from what he'd imagined.
It's only something students shot, so expecting much was unreasonable to begin with.
But everything he'd thought was good while he was shooting it couldn't help looking like trash to him now.
"We'll have to reshoot it..."{p}
rows.12:e9ec:
He told everyone in the society about it.
But they all objected. Redo it, at this point?
"It's just a movie some high schoolers made on their own, isn't it?
No matter how many times you shoot it, it'll come out the same.
Can't you even understand that?
With something like this, what matters is seeing it through, however it turns out."
So said the faculty advisor.
"We worked hard on it, and you call it trash? That kills anyone's motivation."
One of the members spat the words out.
Then, one by one, the ones who'd come to resent Tokita quit.
"This is why amateurs are...
Fine, anyone who wants to quit can go ahead and quit.
Only the ones who really mean it need to stay."
Saying that, Tokita didn't even try to stop them.{p}
rows.12:ec60: Before long, they were finally down to just four people.{p}{a}, would you have stayed?
rows.12:ece8:
You'd stay?
Well, I can understand that.
Tokita was a passionate person.
The ones who stayed in the society must have been moved by his passion too.
Wanting to finish the work with just those of them who were left...
I think Tokita had a kind of charisma.
That must be why they believed in him and stayed, even after he said something so outrageous.{p}
rows.12:ee3c:
Among the members who stayed was Taichi Nakayama, who was in the same year as Tokita and me.
He was the one shooting the film with an 8mm camera.{p}
rows.12:eec8:
Tokita started the reshoot with the ones who were left.
He was careful not to repeat his earlier mistakes.
And he seemed obsessed with the makeup for when the mummy's bandages come off.
There was a scene like that.
He went through trial and error, trying it this way and that.
In the end, they left just that scene unshot and went ahead with the other scenes first.{p}
rows.12:f038:
Then one day, Nakayama came down with a cold and was laid up for about four days.
During that time, Tokita did the filming.
He seemed fairly confident in his own camera skills, too.
Then Nakayama got over his cold, and it seems the shooting wrapped without a hitch.{p}
rows.12:f120:
But just as they were about to start editing, Nakayama announced he was quitting the society.
The shooting was over, so that was enough, he said.
It seems he'd stayed in the society planning that from the start.{p}What do you think Tokita did?
rows.12:f220: He told him he could quit
rows.12:f250:
"You too... Why?
Please, I'm begging you, won't you at least help with the editing...?
There are things only you can do."
Tokita got down on his knees and bowed his head to the floor before him.
Nakayama didn't know what to do.
"Even if you say that..."
He judged that for now, nothing he said would get through to Tokita.
So he decided to cleverly talk Tokita around.
"...All right. We're both passionate about film, after all."
Even as he said that, Nakayama was planning to slip away when he got the chance.
And Tokita happily started the editing with him.
They'd both loved movies to begin with, after all.
For all his complaining, Nakayama seemed to be enjoying himself too.{p}
rows.12:f4c0:
The two of them kept editing until late in the evening, trying it this way and that.
Then one day after school, Tokita came up to me and said this.{p}
rows.12:f568:
"I just finished editing the film the other day.
This is a masterpiece, no doubt about it.
It's going to be a film for the history books.
...You like movies, right?
If you want, I could show you a little of the film's big selling point."
That's how I came to hear about this film.{p}{a}, would you want to see it?
rows.12:f688: I don't need to see it
rows.12:f698:
Right?
Of course you'd want to see it.
I happily tagged along after him, too.
...Anyone who loves movies would be dying to know.{p}
rows.12:f7e0:
"All right, I'm only showing you the film's selling point, but you'll get plenty out of it."
I'd never seen an amateur film before, so I was a little nervous.
First, he told me the outline of the story.
After all, I wasn't going to watch the whole thing.{p}
rows.12:f8c4:
"This is where the coffin arrives in Japan and the mummy awakens for the first time.
And this is the scene where the mummy wanders through the darkness, searching for the princess's reincarnation."
I was astonished.
Yes, from his skillful camerawork right down to the special-effects makeup, it was all so good...
Of course, you can't compare it to an ordinary film released in theaters.
The mummy's makeup especially was the part he'd been most obsessive about, after all.
The bandages had peeled away a little, just around the face, and the dry, flaky skin peeking through, even its color, looked absolutely real.{p}
rows.12:fabc:
"It's amazing.
I'm actually a little moved."
I said that and looked at him.
"Isn't it☆
It was worth all the trouble☆"
As he said that, something about him seemed different from usual.
Then he started saying strange things, one after another.
"Of course it's amazing. It's based on a real, living human being."
"...★"
I didn't quite understand what he meant.{p}
rows.12:fc30:
Then I looked at the screen, and a close-up of the mummy's face came on.
Looking closely at the mummy's face, I got the feeling it was panicking.
Its mouth was flapping open and shut.
It seemed to be saying something.
rows.12:fcec:
There was background music on, so I couldn't hear the voice clearly.
It bothered me a little, so I tried mouthing along with it.
"H... e... l... p..."
I wondered what that was about.
This wasn't a story about a mummy calling for help.
Just then, Tokita spoke.{p}
rows.12:fe08:
"It was hard work.
When you get right down to it, nothing beats a real human.
You pour sulfuric acid on a living person's face and melt it into goo, right?
Then you mix some paints and coat the face with them.
And while you dry it crusty with a hair dryer..."
Listening to his explanation, I was stunned.
Come to think of it, maybe that mummy earlier hadn't been acting, but really wandering around begging for help...
And the mummy had looked like someone, I thought.
"Tokita, I'm sorry, but this isn't a movie☆
It's a crime☆"{p}
rows.12:ffb0:
I'd shouted it before I knew it.
Tokita's eyes glared at me sharply.{p}What would you do at a time like this, {a}?
rows.12:1001c: Make him see it's a crime
rows.12:1003c:
I didn't back down.
"Tokita, get a grip☆
Wake up☆
What you're doing is a crime☆"
Still glaring at me, Tokita said this.
"So you're going to find fault with what I do too?
Hmph. That Nakayama had the gall to run his mouth while we were editing, saying 'This is as good as it'll ever get.'
So I was just aiming for something better.
Do you want to end up like Nakayama too★"
That mummy was Nakayama.
Now that he'd said it, there really was a resemblance.
It seems there'd been some kind of trouble between the two of them.
Tokita edged closer to me.{p}
rows.12:10254:
Then he pulled a small bottle out of his pocket.
"No... s-sulfuric acid★"
I screamed.
"You're gonna be material for my special-effects makeup too☆"
He lunged at me.{p}
rows.12:1030c: At that moment, Nakayama, who'd been wandering inside the film, leapt out of the darkness of the screen.
rows.12:10414: Then he snatched the small bottle from Tokita's hand, unscrewed the cap and made him drink it.
rows.12:10470:
"Uggggghhhhh!"
Blood running from his mouth, Tokita clawed at his throat.{p}
rows.12:104c8: Mixed in with the red blood, he coughed up white, gooey filth in wet, choking gulps...
rows.12:10514: He thrashed around, and soon he stopped moving.{p}
rows.12:10618:
No one would believe a story like this, no matter who I told.
I decided that I hadn't seen anything, and hadn't heard anything.
I heard Nakayama's body was found in the basement under the P.E. equipment shed.
The official story was that he'd been killed after an argument with Tokita.
As for Tokita, it seems the story was that, tormented by his conscience, he poisoned himself.
Yes, the decisive evidence was that film.
Apparently, the film had even recorded the whole process of Tokita giving Nakayama his special-effects makeup.{p}
rows.12:107e8:
Even now, whenever I see a white screen, I feel like I might catch a glimpse of Nakayama.
People who get too obsessed are frightening, aren't they?
My story ends here.
So we're finally down to the last one.
Now, next person... go ahead.{p}
rows.12:108b0:
You'd give up on the editing?
I see. If someone involved in an amateur production died, I can understand having second thoughts.
He was very disappointed too, having finally founded the Film Research Society he'd longed for and gotten to the point of making a film.
But he was a warm-hearted person, so he decided to give up editing the film.
Besides, he also felt uneasy about editing a film that showed someone who'd been murdered.{p}
rows.12:10b44:
"The last time I was in the audiovisual room was last Saturday.
I'm sure I put all the editing equipment away then..."
After all, the only people with a key to this room were the teacher and him...
And the teacher would never do something like that.
But he chose to look on the bright side.
Surely this was the student who'd played the detective, who'd met such a bitter end, begging him to finish the film...
There's no doubt he himself had plenty of lingering regrets about having to stop editing halfway.
Partly for that reason, he got right to work on the editing.{p}
rows.12:10d4c:
{a}, you're quite a cold person, aren't you?
Well, it's true that with words alone, anyone can make big claims.
I understand that you can't really say until you've actually seen it.
But he said it with tremendous confidence.
If you'd been there, {a}, I think his intensity, his pushiness, would have won you over, and you'd have gone to see it.
There was just something about what he said that really drew you in.{p}
